cases.title: Bharatmala: who independently challenged the project?
cases.question: Did delegated appraisal and inconsistent project/package units reduce independent scrutiny before large commitments?
cases.finding: CAG documents a scrutiny gap: NHAI internally approved large EPC schemes and used inconsistent project/package units. MoRTH offered technical and EPC-design explanations; the record does not establish collusion or a quantified loss.

geography.label: Delhi
geography.basis: Dwarka corridor case association and Union decision-making location

claims.text: CAG found non-separation of execution, appraisal and approval roles and inconsistent treatment of projects and packages.
claims.response: No MoRTH reply was recorded to certain delegation observations; its technical responses are retained separately.
claims.alternative: Delegated EPC decision-making can expedite delivery without implying bidder influence.
claims.falsifier: A contemporaneous independent appraisal and legally consistent project definition for the cited decisions would narrow this concern.

claims.text: The ₹250.77 crore/km project civil-cost figure and ₹18.20 crore/km programme-category norm do not establish a like-for-like loss.
claims.response: MoRTH defended elevated traffic segregation and EPC design scope; CAG disputed the recorded alternatives analysis.
claims.alternative: Urban elevated structures, interchanges and design scope can explain substantial cost differences.
claims.falsifier: A reconciled same-scope cost estimate, quantities and final payment audit could quantify a defensible difference.

whatWeKnow: CAG identifies 35 of 50 sampled NHAI projects with tender notices before technical/financial appraisal and 46 with approval after tender notice; this is the audit sample, not a national prevalence rate.
For HAM Vadodara–Mumbai Phase IA, CAG says package-level treatment avoided the approval level required for a single combined project; this must not be misdescribed as the EPC rule for Dwarka.
Package 4 has a named contractor and award value; no payment or covert recipient is identified.
Later official opening announcements provide evidence of delivery, not an independent benefits evaluation.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether a specific design/appraisal departure favoured any bidder rather than reflected an engineering or governance choice.
Whether independent scrutiny occurred outside the records available to CAG.
Final same-scope costs, operating outcomes and signed audit-action closure.

nextRecords.record: CCEA note, mode-specific approval rules, Board and PATSC minutes for each package
nextRecords.purpose: Reconstruct authority and sequence without conflating EPC and HAM thresholds.

nextRecords.record: Dated alternatives analysis, tender BOQ, bid evaluations and final payment certificates
nextRecords.purpose: Test disproportionate advantage and reconcile approval, award and payment stages.

limits: No conspiracy finding, pooled loss or bidder-politician transfer is supported.
2017–2018 decisions are reconstructed from later audit; private motives and a complete archived information set are unknown.

actors.authority: Delegate and exercise project appraisal/approval within the formal programme.
actors.incentive: Institutional incentive to deliver quickly while controlling engineering and financial risk; not a claim of actual personal motive.

actors.authority: Set programme policy and respond to the audit.
actors.incentive: Institutional incentive to relieve congestion and demonstrate delivery, alongside duty to justify design and expenditure.

informationThen.text: October 2017 programme approval and mode-dependent appraisal rules were the relevant framework; CAG later reconstructs the November delegation.
The 2023 audit and 2025 opening were not known outcomes at the 2017 decision.

options.label: Obtain an independent corridor-wide review before commitments
options.expectedObservableOutcome: A dated review would compare design alternatives, total corridor cost and appropriate authority.

options.label: Use formally delegated EPC approval with explicit documented reasons
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Minutes would show applicable powers, independent participation and engineering trade-offs.

options.label: Pause unresolved appraisals and revise the project definition
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Award timetable could lengthen while approval and scope ambiguity is resolved.

decisionAnalysis.observedOutcome: CAG recorded internal approvals, absent DPRs and inconsistent units, with MoRTH technical rebuttal; by August 2025 the government reported both sections opened.
hindsightLimits: Retrospective institutional scenario analysis, not a solved game or evidence of a shared illicit strategy.
Authority and technical risk differ between EPC, HAM and agencies.

hypothesis.proposition: The combination of internal approvals and inconsistent project/package units weakened independent challenge of large road commitments; whether that favoured particular firms remains unproved.
hypothesis.assessmentReason: The narrow scrutiny pattern is documented in CAG’s sample. The reviewed record does not identify an agreement with a contractor, improper payment or comparable-cost loss.
hypothesis.jurisdiction: Union MoRTH/NHAI/CCEA programme decisions; Haryana supplied land and local interface, but that does not assign it every Union approval.

rules.title: Bharatmala CCEA appraisal and delegation framework
rules.operativePeriod: October–November 2017 framework applicable to the audited approvals
rules.requirement: Appraisal/approval levels varied by implementation agency and construction mode; CAG identifies ambiguity over project versus package.

rules.title: MoRTH Bharatmala Standard Operating Procedure
rules.operativePeriod: December 2017; consider its exact timing for each December 2017/2018 appraisal
rules.requirement: CAG states the SOP required judicious DPR preparation and guidance; MoRTH argued EPC feasibility/tender drawings were sufficient.

alternatives.label: Unproved preferential coordination
alternatives.explanation: Approval gaps may have reduced scrutiny of choices favourable to particular suppliers; no evidence of agreement is obtained.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Contemporaneous correspondence, conflict disclosures and bid-level deviations tied to a named award.

alternatives.label: Lawful delivery and engineering trade-offs
alternatives.explanation: Delegation and elevated design may reflect congestion, safety and faster EPC delivery.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Dated alternatives analysis and independently reviewed life-cycle costs.

alternatives.label: Incomparable units and incomplete records
alternatives.explanation: Programme averages, road-km, lane-km, civil cost and later total section cost may be conflated.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: A reconciled package/corridor register using identical scope, price date and financial stage.

tests.question: Were the required technical/financial appraisal and approval completed before the notice inviting tender?
tests.expectedIfTrue: Required appraisal or approval follows tender publication in the cited sample, reducing scrutiny before inviting bids.
tests.expectedIfAlternative: Dated pre-tender appraisal/approval exists, or the applicable rules expressly permit a documented exception.
tests.observation: CAG reports 35/50 sampled NHAI tender notices before appraisal and 46/50 approvals 7–404 days after tender notice. These dates do not establish appraisal or approval after contract award; actual commitment dates remain unjoined.
tests.nextRecord: Original dated appraisal/approval minutes, tender notices, award dates and applicable exception authority for each sampled decision

tests.question: Did the disputed design generate an unjustified awardee advantage after matching engineering scope?
tests.expectedIfTrue: Same-scope comparisons and evaluation records show unexplained favourable departures connected to the awardee.
tests.expectedIfAlternative: Independent design assessment, competitive bids and costs explain the difference without preferential treatment.
tests.observation: MoRTH technical reasons and later delivery exist; comparable BOQs, payment ledger and independent review are missing.
tests.nextRecord: Same-scope design comparator, bids, BOQs, change orders and payments

proposedLinks.question: Did any appraisal departure specifically advantage the Package 4 awardee?
proposedLinks.missingEvidence: Award-specific evaluation, correspondence and quantified causal link between departure and advantage.
proposedLinks.disconfirmingEvidence: Consistent criteria across bidders and independent same-scope justification with no preferential intervention.

chronology.event: NHAI Board delegated EPC appraisal/approval powers, following October 2017 CCEA programme approval.
PIB announced the Package 4 award. The audit separately places the four-package approval cohort in January–March 2018; individual dates are not joined here.
CAG audit tabled, including MoRTH April 2022 replies.
PMO reported Delhi opening, with Haryana section already opened in March 2024.

hypothesis.comparison: Match EPC with EPC by urban complexity, structures, terrain, scope, price date and approval date; use NHIDCL/MoRTH as governance comparators only after adjustment. Do not choose only overrunning projects or divide project cost by a programme mean.
inferenceLimits: Retrospective reconstruction, not a preregistered prediction.
Supported pattern refers to an oversight arrangement, not corruption, conspiracy or a causal effect estimate.
Contrary delivery and engineering evidence remain visible.

cases.title: Grants: does missing certification change the next release?
cases.question: Are recurring grants screened against overdue utilisation certificates consistently across ministries and recipients?
cases.period: FY2021–22 to FY2023–24 recent cohort; older outstanding balances explicitly dated back to FY1985–86
cases.finding: CAG’s FY2025 accounts audit establishes persistent certification gaps across 15 reporting ministries. Whether particular recipients received improper fresh releases remains untested: the public table lacks grant IDs, recipients and payment dates.

geography.label: Union ministries, New Delhi
geography.basis: Accountability-holder location; underlying beneficiaries and projects are geographically unresolved

claims.text: CAG reports 33,973 outstanding UCs covering ₹54,282.32 crore from 15 reporting ministries/departments, with mixed temporal scope.
claims.response: Ministries reported follow-up; Education said it had developed an IT monitoring system.
claims.alternative: Late documentation, unreconciled balances or legacy grants can produce outstanding UCs without diversion.
claims.falsifier: Grant-level reconciled returns and accepted certificates would establish how much of the stock is actually unresolved.
missingRecords: Amounts and age bands using one cutoff

claims.text: The audit’s outstanding UC amount is not a finding that ₹54,282.32 crore was stolen or transferred to NGOs or politicians.
claims.response: CAG calls for timely certification and PFMS integration; it does not identify those illicit recipients.
claims.alternative: Services or assets may have been delivered even where certification is overdue.
claims.falsifier: A specific payment trail plus verified non-delivery or adjudicated diversion could support a separate bounded finding.

whatWeKnow: The table covers the 15 departments/ministries that furnished information, not a census of every ministry or a random sample of offenders.
13,926 UCs / ₹38,287.52 crore are reported for FY2021–22 to FY2023–24, but Agriculture and AYUSH did not furnish separate recent-cohort totals.
AYUSH’s 1,622 UCs / ₹2,403.25 crore use a 16 September 2025 cutoff despite the table’s 31 March 2025 heading.
Higher Education’s recent cohort is 2,934 UCs / ₹14,218.20 crore; Housing’s is 1,034 / ₹14,681.86 crore. Counts and amounts measure different workloads.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether any named recipient received a fresh recurring grant contrary to the applicable UC condition.
Which outstanding records reflect delivery failures, administrative delay, reconciliation or lawful exceptions.
A complete ministry denominator and same-cohort baseline over successive years.

nextRecords.record: De-identified grant register joining sanction ID, recipient legal ID, recurring/non-recurring classification, due date, accepted UC and next release
nextRecords.holder: Selected ministries / PFMS / Controller General of Accounts
nextRecords.purpose: Test release-condition compliance on identical grant cohorts.

nextRecords.record: Action Taken Notes and independently checked asset/service completion records
nextRecords.holder: MoHUA / Education / Health / CAG liaison divisions
nextRecords.purpose: Distinguish certification backlog from failed delivery and evaluate responses.

limits: No named covert beneficiary or new cash-flow link is supported.
Older accumulated balances predate May 2014; they cannot all be attributed to a single administration.
Rule 238 is applied to the post-2017 recent cohort; older grants require their own contemporaneous rule and sanction terms.

actors.authority: Monitor UCs and authorise grants within applicable sanction terms.
actors.incentive: Institutional tension between continued services and complete financial assurance; this is an analytic incentive, not proof of misconduct.

actors.authority: Oversee urban grant programmes and outstanding recipient certification.
actors.incentive: Institutional incentive to deliver projects while enforcing release controls; exact recipient-level choices unknown.

actors.authority: Audit Union accounts and report compliance gaps.
actors.incentive: Institutional mandate to improve evidence of authorised use, not to assign criminal guilt from missing forms.

informationThen.text: For each FY2021–22 to FY2023–24 recurring grant decision, the previous year’s UC status and sanction conditions should be relevant; the actual decision files were not obtained.

options.label: Apply the release conditions with documented UC verification
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Release files contain accepted certificates/audited accounts and checks appropriate to the tranche.

options.label: Resolve backlog and lawful exceptions transparently
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Registers distinguish exceptional authority, time limits and pending documentation from ordinary compliant releases.

options.label: Withhold a noncompliant tranche while addressing service continuity
options.expectedObservableOutcome: A documented hold and remediation pathway would be observable; withholding alone is not evidence of better welfare outcomes.

decisionAnalysis.observedOutcome: CAG reports recurring certification pendency and recorded ministry follow-up/IT monitoring; no recipient-level fresh-release decisions are established.
hindsightLimits: No single release decision date is invented for an aggregate stock.
Recent and legacy cohorts, recurring and non-recurring grants, and service continuity require separate treatment.

hypothesis.proposition: Fragmented grant and UC registers may permit inconsistent enforcement of release conditions; whether this systematically favoured particular grantees is an open question.
hypothesis.assessmentReason: The certification backlog is documented, but a recipient-level join from overdue UC to later release is missing. The audit table cannot establish selective exemption or diversion.
hypothesis.jurisdiction: Union sanctioning ministries and reporting systems; grantees may include state/public/autonomous bodies. State/NGO/private recipient identity is unresolved.

rules.title: General Financial Rules 2017, Rule 238(1) and (2), as reproduced by CAG
rules.operativePeriod: 2017 rule cited for the examined FY2021–22 to FY2023–24 cohort; obtain version and sanction terms per release
rules.requirement: Non-recurring UCs are due within 12 months after financial-year end; recurring releases require preceding-year UC and releases above 75% require UC plus annual audited statement, as described in the audit.

alternatives.label: Unproved selective release
alternatives.explanation: Similar overdue recipients might receive different treatment through discretionary exceptions; no recipient is identified here.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Same-scheme grant-level next-release decisions, rule basis and exception approvals.

alternatives.label: Delivery with administrative backlog
alternatives.explanation: Projects may operate while certificates are delayed or valid exception procedures apply.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Physical/service verification, signed exception authority and subsequent accepted UCs.

alternatives.label: Cohort or cutoff mismatch
alternatives.explanation: Legacy records, a different AYUSH cutoff and missing recent-cohort subtotals can distort comparisons.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Reconciled common-date register with grant type, financial year and recipient identifiers.

tests.question: Were fresh recurring grants released without the required previous-year assurance?
tests.expectedIfTrue: A dated, identifiable recurring release occurs after the required UC deadline with no UC or lawful basis.
tests.expectedIfAlternative: The certificate was accepted before release, grant type differed, or a valid documented authority applied.
tests.observation: Only ministry aggregates and rule text were obtained; the required grant-ID join is absent.

tests.question: Does the apparent concentration persist on the same cohort and cutoff?
tests.expectedIfTrue: Large gaps remain for comparable grants and distinguish differential treatment after workload adjustment.
tests.expectedIfAlternative: Reconciliation, recent certificates or denominator correction substantially reduce the disparity.
tests.observation: CAG explicitly flags AYUSH’s different cutoff and two missing recent-cohort subtotals; blanket cross-ministry rankings are not reliable.
tests.nextRecord: All-ministry same-date returns and comparable recent-cohort release totals
tests.holder: Controller General of Accounts / reporting ministries

proposedLinks.question: Did any unidentified overdue grantee receive a subsequent recurring release without the required assurance?
proposedLinks.missingEvidence: Recipient legal ID, grant ID, UC due/acceptance dates, release date and applicable exception authority.
proposedLinks.disconfirmingEvidence: Certificate accepted before release, no new release, non-recurring classification or lawful documented exception.

chronology.event: Main reported snapshot of outstanding UCs; legacy balances extend before 2014.
AYUSH row uses this later cutoff, a source footnote that limits aggregation.
CAG report signed after recording ministry responses.
Union Accounts FY2024–25 report tabled in Parliament.

hypothesis.comparison: Compare identical grant types, recipient classes, size bands, due dates and years, with fresh releases as denominator. Include compliant recipients and pre-2014/earlier cohorts separately; do not treat the 15 reporting ministries as every ministry.
inferenceLimits: Retrospective reconstruction, not a preregistered prediction.
Certification stock is not a loss estimate or a flow to an identified private beneficiary.
Audit and ministry replies are one source family; no independent bank-trail corroboration.

cases.title: Pegasus: separate secrecy, device findings and operator identity
cases.question: Can the oversight record distinguish legitimate confidentiality from withholding that prevents verification of unlawful surveillance?
cases.period: 2018 allegations as context; 2021–2025 proceedings inspected; current-docket gap through 14 October 2026
cases.finding: The 2021 Court order establishes an insufficient disclosure response and an independent inquiry. Reported 2022 device results were inconclusive on Pegasus; 2025 disclosure disputes do not identify the operator, procurement route or a minister’s culpability.

geography.label: Supreme Court and Union respondent, New Delhi
geography.basis: Proceeding and institutional location; not the location of devices, targets or surveillance infrastructure

claims.text: The Court held the Union’s limited affidavit insufficient and required asserted secrecy to be justified; it ordered an inquiry rather than deciding operator identity.
claims.response: The Union denied allegations, cited lawful interception safeguards and offered its own committee.
claims.alternative: Some secrecy can legitimately protect operations or private device data; it is not automatically obstruction.
claims.falsifier: A specific later merits order or reasoned disclosure ruling could settle or narrow the outstanding questions.

claims.text: The 2022 hearing report does not establish that five examined phones were infected with Pegasus or that the Union bought it.
claims.response: Reporting describes no conclusive Pegasus evidence in 29 examined phones and preserves the government’s response to the non-cooperation observation.
claims.alternative: Other malware, limited artifacts or sample selection can account for inconclusive findings.
claims.falsifier: An authenticated device-specific forensic conclusion plus a separate operator attribution could support a narrower claim.

whatWeKnow: The Court’s inquiry expressly asked whether Union, state or other entities acquired or used the spyware and under what law; asking the question is not answering it.
The Union’s original affidavit expressly denied allegations and described interception oversight.
The 2022 report is a secondary account of oral readings from a sealed report; its inconclusive finding and non-cooperation statement must both remain visible.
The 2025 hearing source records competing disclosure arguments, not a final judgment identifying an operator.
whatWeDoNotKnow: The sealed technical report, device-to-case matching and full chain of custody.
A source-supported Indian procurement contract, paying entity, operator, authorisation or beneficiary for the claimed activity.
Whether a later order after April 2025 changed disclosure or merits; no such original obtained in this bounded search.

limits: Non-cooperation is not proof of spyware procurement, attack sponsorship or a false-flag operation.
A target-list entry, confirmed infection, operator attribution and legality are distinct propositions.
No nonpublic files were accessed and no operational evasion, surveillance or hacking procedure is provided.

actors.authority: Protect rights, evaluate secrecy justifications and constitute an independent inquiry.
actors.incentive: Institutional incentive to obtain credible evidence while avoiding release of private or security-sensitive data.

actors.incentive: Institutional incentive to preserve evidentiary reliability, access and individual privacy.

informationThen.text: At the October 2021 decision, petitions, expert material and the Union’s limited affidavit were before the Court; the 2022 report and 2025 debate were later outcomes.

options.label: Provide court-supervised, appropriately protected evidence
options.expectedObservableOutcome: A reasoned disclosure record could allow technical/operator questions to be tested while protecting sensitive material.

options.label: Maintain a specific, judicially justified confidentiality claim
options.expectedObservableOutcome: The record would identify lawful reasons, scope and less restrictive disclosure possibilities.

options.label: Use an independent technical inquiry
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Written terms, cooperation directions and findings would separate device evidence from legal/operator questions.

decisionAnalysis.observedOutcome: Independent inquiry was ordered. Subsequent reporting describes inconclusive device findings, claimed non-cooperation and continuing debate over report access.
hindsightLimits: Retrospective comparison of institutional choices, not a claim to know classified evidence or private intentions.
No operator or unlawful purpose is inferred from confidentiality, officeholding, vendor nationality or shared timing.

hypothesis.proposition: Broad confidentiality positions may leave important surveillance-accountability questions untestable in public; whether they concealed unlawful domestic deployment is not established.
hypothesis.assessmentReason: The disclosure concern has judicial support, but the stronger covert-acquisition or unlawful-deployment theory lacks a verified operator/payment link and must contend with inconclusive reported device findings.
hypothesis.jurisdiction: Union respondent and Supreme Court inquiry; order also contemplated state or other operators. Do not assign all possible surveillance to the Union or MeitY merely because it filed the affidavit.

rules.title: Article 21 privacy and judicial review of secrecy claims in the 27 October 2021 order
rules.operativePeriod: Constitutional principles applied at the 2021 inquiry decision
rules.requirement: Security considerations may justify withholding, but the Court required specific grounds and proof; a prima facie inquiry is not a merits finding.

rules.title: Court’s inquiry and cooperation directions
rules.requirement: Investigate acquisition, use, legal authority and affected persons; Union, states and agencies were directed to cooperate.

alternatives.label: Unproved concealment of misuse
alternatives.explanation: Overbroad secrecy might prevent review of unlawful surveillance; no specific unlawful deployment is established here.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: An authenticated device incident linked to an operator and absent or unlawful authorisation.

alternatives.label: Legitimate confidentiality and privacy
alternatives.explanation: Restricted circulation may protect national-security information and private device contents while permitting supervised review.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Specific judicially accepted reasons and a meaningful redacted or device-specific review pathway.

alternatives.label: Forensic or identity mismatch
alternatives.explanation: Potential-target lists, malware artifacts, devices examined and actual Pegasus operators may refer to different populations.
alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Chain-of-custody device mapping, reproducible findings and independent operator attribution.
